verses.text: Paul came to Derbe and then Lystra. A disciple named Timothy lived there. His mother was a Jewish believer, and his father was Greek.
The believers in Lystra and Iconium spoke well of Timothy.
Paul wanted Timothy to travel with him, so he circumcised him because of the Jews in that area. Everyone knew his father was Greek.
As they traveled from town to town, they delivered the decisions made by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem for the churches to follow.
So the churches grew stronger in faith and gained more people every day.
They traveled through the regions of Phrygia and Galatia, but the Holy Spirit stopped them from preaching the message in Asia.
When they reached the border of Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus wouldn’t let them.
So they passed through Mysia and went down to Troas.
That night Paul saw a vision: a man from Macedonia was standing there, pleading, “Come over to Macedonia and help us!”
After Paul saw the vision, we got ready at once to leave for Macedonia. We concluded that God had called us to share the good news with them.
We sailed from Troas straight to Samothrace. The next day we reached Neapolis,
and from there we went to Philippi, a leading city in that part of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We stayed there for several days.
On the Sabbath we went outside the city gate to the riverside, where we thought there might be a place of prayer. We sat down and spoke with the women who had gathered there.
One of them was Lydia, a seller of purple cloth from Thyatira who worshiped God. The Lord opened her heart to pay close attention to Paul’s message.
She and everyone in her household were baptized. Then she urged us, “If you believe I’m faithful to the Lord, come stay at my house.” She wouldn’t take no for an answer.
One day, as we were heading to the place of prayer, a slave girl met us. She had a spirit that let her predict the future, and her owners made a lot of money from her fortune-telling.
She followed Paul and us, shouting, “These men serve the Most High God! They’re telling you how to be saved!”
She kept doing this for many days. Finally Paul was fed up, so he turned to the spirit and said, “In the name of Jesus Christ, I command you: come out of her!” The spirit left her immediately.
When her owners realized their chance to make money was gone, they grabbed Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace to face the officials.
They brought them before the magistrates and accused them: “These men are Jews, and they’re stirring up trouble in our city.
“They’re promoting customs that we Romans aren’t allowed to accept or practice!”
The crowd joined in against them. The magistrates tore off their clothes and ordered them beaten with rods.
After a severe beating, Paul and Silas were thrown into prison. The jailer was ordered to guard them carefully.
He got that order, put them in the inner cell, and locked their feet in stocks.
Around midnight, Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, while the other prisoners listened. 🎶
Suddenly a powerful earthquake shook the prison foundations. Every door flew open, and everyone’s chains came loose.
The jailer woke up and saw the doors open. He drew his sword and was about to kill himself, thinking the prisoners had escaped.
But Paul shouted, “Don’t hurt yourself! We’re all still here!”
The jailer called for lights, rushed inside, and fell trembling at Paul and Silas’s feet.
Then he led them out and asked, “Sirs, what do I need to do to be saved?”
They answered, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you’ll be saved—you and everyone in your household.”
Then they shared the Lord’s message with him and everyone in his home.
At that same hour of the night, the jailer washed their wounds. Then he and everyone in his household were baptized right away.
He brought them into his home, served them a meal, and celebrated with his whole household because they had come to believe in God.
When morning came, the magistrates sent officers with this message: “Let those men go.”
The jailer told Paul, “The magistrates say you’re free to leave. Go in peace.”

But Paul said, “They beat us in public without a trial, even though we’re Roman citizens, and threw us in prison. Now they want to release us quietly? No way! Let them come here themselves and escort us out.”
The officers reported this to the magistrates. When they heard Paul and Silas were Roman citizens, they were alarmed.
They came and apologized to them. Then they escorted them out and asked them to leave the city.
After leaving the prison, Paul and Silas went to Lydia’s house. They met with the believers there and encouraged them, then left.
